requirements.requirement: /srv/drop created on node1 as a shared writable directory (world-writable, mode 1777, root:root)
requirements.summary: cmd-d9c4d0b6a3734f22 shows mkdir, chown root:root, chmod 1777, and stat/ls confirming '1777 root:root /srv/drop' / 'drwxrwxrwt'. Multiple distinct unprivileged users (dropuserA, testC, testE, testG, testH, dropuserX) successfully created files in the directory both before and after restart, directly demonstrating shared write access.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky-bit enforcement), while owners can still delete their own files
requirements.summary: cmd-d9c4d0b6a3734f22 shows dropuserB's rm attempt on dropuserA's file failing with 'Operation not permitted' while dropuserA (owner) successfully deletes it. Re-verified after restart with fresh users dropuserX/dropuserY in cmd-08529ce282e74b78, showing identical blocked-delete behavior.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is durable/persists (verified by executor via mandatory restart evidence protocol)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline (boot_id 1e0cb179...) and post-restart state (boot_id c998a427..., a genuinely different boot identity, confirmed via connection timeout during reboot then successful reconnection) show /srv/drop retained mode 1777 root:root and sticky-bit deletion protection intact after a real reboot, satisfying the restart evidence protocol for this task's single managed node.

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes - a shared, world-writable /srv/drop with sticky-bit protection so only file owners (or root) can delete their own files - are directly and repeatedly demonstrated with multiple distinct users, both before and after a genuine node reboot (proven via differing boot identifiers). The executor also completed the independent node-restart evidence protocol correctly for node1. Hygiene is good but not perfect: an unresolved side investigation into an unrelated permission anomaly consumed six extra test users/files (fully reverted), and one stray /tmp/err.log file was left behind.
limitations: The cause of the transient 'Permission denied' anomaly when writing into an existing 666 file was never conclusively explained, only attributed to a 'timing flake'; this does not affect the core directory/sticky-bit requirement but leaves a loose end in the evidence trail.

No lifecycle diff for the after_prepare phase was available since prepare was disabled (after_prepare is an alias of before_prepare), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on the executor_comparison against before_prepare.

operational_hygiene.summary: Core configuration was minimal and correct (mkdir/chown/chmod), and all test artifacts inside /srv/drop plus all test users (dropuserA/B, testC-H, dropuserX/Y) were removed by cleanup command cmd-950c8d49f3534fa1 and within cmd-08529ce282e74b78, leaving /srv/drop empty with correct permissions in the final after_executor snapshot. However, the executor ran an extended sequence of troubleshooting experiments (cmd-dccbea093e9d445b, cmd-8ca700367a544288, cmd-7e96834064234bd5, cmd-4f10c5501a204c17) creating/deleting six additional test users and files (testC-testH) to chase an anomalous 'Permission denied' result on writing into an existing file owned by another user - a scenario governed by standard per-file permission bits, not the directory's sticky-bit configuration being verified. These mutations were bounded and fully reverted, so they are treated as low-severity unnecessary mutations rather than residue. One low-risk mutation was left in place: /tmp/err.log, created by the stderr redirection in cmd-08529ce282e74b78's post-restart delete test, is visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was never cleaned up.
